docs.title: Rational tangles
docs.text:
This blueprint formalizes Conway's classification of rational tangles, following the integral-coloring proof of Kauffman and Lambropoulou §5 together with the form lemmas of §§2–3 and Theorem 3.

docs.title: Coverage
docs.text:
Coverage is tracked at chapter level. The first milestone is Conway's classification of rational tangles (Kauffman–Lambropoulou, Theorem 1), proved via the integral coloring of §5. Rows span that theorem, the rest of the adopted paper, and the Conway census the user placed out of scope. The labels below are validated Autoform dispositions: MAPPED, DECOMPOSED, DEFERRED, or OUT.

docs.title: Completion rule
docs.text: The current milestone is complete when the classification node and every article it depends on compile under recorded Lean declarations and pass mathematical and code review. That includes the coloring lemmas of §5 and does not include Tait, Schubert's theorems, or the Conway census.

docs.title: Rational tangles roadmap
docs.text: The long-term interest of this area is the role of rational tangles in the enumeration of knots and links. The first milestone is intentionally a single theorem: rational tangles are equivalent if and only if their continued-fraction fractions are equal.

docs.title: High-level map
docs.text: 1. Rational tangles — Reidemeister moves, 2-tangles, integer and rational tangles, flypes and flips, continued- fraction form, the tangle fraction \(F\), the integral coloring of §5, and Conway's classification.

docs.title: Current milestone
docs.text:
Formalize the definitions through Kauffman–Lambropoulou Theorem 1 (Conway, 1970), proving Theorem 2 via the coloring fraction of §5 (Theorem 4) rather than via Tait flyping and Proposition 4. Keep Theorem 3 from §4. The coverage page records what the project does and does not yet claim.

→ NextRational tangles

docs.title: Rational tangles
docs.text: This chapter isolates the combinatorial theory of rational 2-tangles used by Kauffman and Lambropoulou to prove Conway's classification. It begins with Reidemeister moves, 2-tangles and isotopy, builds integer and rational tangles and the flype/flip moves, then matches continued-fraction form of a tangle with the arithmetic continued fraction of its fraction \(F(T)\). The execution plan for the classification is the integral-coloring argument of §5: a coloring fraction \(f\) is a topological invariant and equals \(F\), so \(F\) is an isotopy invariant (Theorem 2) without Tait. Theorem 3 (same fraction implies isotopic) is kept from §4. The main result is that two rational tangles are isotopic if and only if they have the same fraction.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text:
A 2-tangle is an embedding of two arcs (and possibly circles) in a 3-ball with four endpoints on the boundary. Diagram isotopy is generated by Reidemeister moves in the interior of the disc. Rational tangles are those generated from \([0]\) or \([\infty]\) by consecutive twists of neighbouring endpoints. Flypes and flips are characteristic isotopies used to reach standard, continued- fraction, and canonical form. The fraction \(F(T)\) is the arithmetical evaluation of the twist form.

The foundations chapter holds the definitions.

docs.title: Forms
docs.text:
Standard form, continued-fraction form, and canonical form are reached by flypes (as isotopies proved in the paper, not via Tait). The arithmetic continued fraction of a rational has a unique canonical form (Proposition 3), which is the numerical counterpart of the tangle canonical form and is used in Theorem 3.

The normal-forms chapter proves the forms, and the toolkit chapter holds the slideReady coloring-fraction lemmas feeding the coloring fraction.

docs.title: Coloring
docs.text: The coloring chapter develops the integral coloring of §5, including the Reidemeister and flype coloring lemmas and Theorem 4.

docs.title: Classification
docs.text:
Theorem 2 follows from Theorem 4 (\(f\) invariant and \(f=F\)). Theorem 3 is unchanged from §4. Theorem 1 is their conjunction.

The classification chapter holds the three capstone results. The §4 flyping alternate (Tait background) lives in the toolkit chapter as exposition, marked out of the coverage contract for this milestone.

← PreviousRational tangles roadmap→ NextTangle foundations

docs.title: The fraction through integral coloring
docs.text:
This nested chapter is the execution plan for Conway's classification: Kauffman–Lambropoulou §5. Color the arcs of a rational tangle by integers so that under-arcs \(\alpha,\gamma\) and over-arc \(\beta\) satisfy \(\alpha+\gamma=2\beta\). The resulting color matrix determines a quantity \(f(T)\) which is a topological invariant, obeys the same arithmetic as the continued-fraction fraction \(F(T)\), and equals \(F(T)\). Theorem 2 (that \(F\) is an isotopy invariant) follows from \(f\) being invariant and \(f=F\), without the Tait flyping conjecture. Combined with §§2–3 and Theorem 3 this proves Theorem 1.

The paper calls Reidemeister (and flype) invariance of the coloring "easy to verify". Those verifications are listed below as lemmas to prove, not as axioms.

Formalization progress3 definitions · 12 results15 fully proved

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text:
Definition1Coloring rule#✓fully proved

Colors are taken from \(\mathbb{Z}\) or from \(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}\) for some \(n\). At a crossing, if two undercrossing arcs colored \(\alpha\) and \(\gamma\) meet an overcrossing arc colored \(\beta\), then $$ \alpha+\gamma=2\beta, $$ equivalently \(\gamma=2\beta-\alpha\) (Kauffman–Lambropoulou §5, Figure 20). One under-arc color is determined by the other under-arc color and the over-arc color.

Write \(\tau_\beta(\alpha):=2\beta-\alpha\) for the operation that produces the remaining under-arc. This is the coloring rule in operational form, used to check Reidemeister invariance.

Dependencies Statement usesInductive 2 (2-tangle and isotopy) Used byStructure 1 (Color matrix) · Lemma 1 (Affine freedom of coloring) · Lemma 2 (Coloring invariance under flypes) · Lemma 6 (Left product by the vertical trivial tangle is planar reindexing) · Lemma 3 (Coloring invariance under Reidemeister I) · Lemma 4 (Coloring invariance under Reidemeister II) · Lemma 5 (Coloring invariance under Reidemeister III) · Theorem 1 (Every rational tangle is integrally colorable) · Theorem 2 (Reversible fragment of coloring isotopy) · Theorem 150 (Reversible coloring isotopy, core) · Theorem 151 (Carrying colorings along reversible isotopy) · Theorem 152 (Local flype and R3 symmetries) · Theorem 153 (Reverse colorings for local moves) · Theorem 154 (Reverse one-way glue) · Theorem 155 (Reverse zero-add) Structure1Color matrix#✓fully proved

Let \(T\) be a colored 2-tangle. Write \(\mathrm{NW}(T)\), \(\mathrm{NE}(T)\), \(\mathrm{SW}(T)\) and \(\mathrm{SE}(T)\) for the colors on the external strands at the northwest, northeast, southwest and southeast positions. The color matrix of \(T\) is $$ M(T)=\begin{pmatrix}\mathrm{NW}(T)&\mathrm{NE}(T)\\mathrm{SW}(T)&\mathrm{SE}(T)\end{pmatrix}. $$

Dependencies Statement usesDefinition 1 (Coloring rule) · Inductive 2 (2-tangle and isotopy) Used byDefinition 2 (Coloring fraction) · Lemma 1 (Affine freedom of coloring) · Lemma 2 (Coloring invariance under flypes) · Theorem 3 (Coloring fraction of a rational tangle) · Lemma 6 (Left product by the vertical trivial tangle is planar reindexing) Definition2Coloring fraction#✓fully proved

Let \(T\) be an integrally colored 2-tangle with color matrix \(M=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}\). The coloring fraction is the extended rational $$ f(T):=\frac{b-a}{b-d}, $$ with the convention \(f(T)=\infty=1/0\) when \(b=d\) and \(b\neq a\). (If \(T\) is colored but not rational, the same formula is used, but the value may depend on the choice of coloring.)

docs.title: Formalization status
docs.text:
Parts (1) and (3)–(7) are formalized as the theorem4_* wrappers in ColoringFractionTheorem.lean, each proved by the lemma named in its docstring: (1) diagonal sum on standard forms, now extended to every coloring of every diagram with a ColoringIsotopy path from the diagram to a slideReady twist (diagonal_of_ColoringIsotopy_slideReady and the two ReversibleColoringIsotopy variants in DiagonalSumGeneral.lean); (3) additivity under the glue-port (S.NW ≠ S.SW) and diagonal hypotheses (plus the coloring_fraction_mul dual, with its own glue-port and diagonal hypotheses); (4) -1/F on mirror-invert of slideReady twists; (5) -F on the mirror of slideReady twists; (6) 1/F carried by the inverse of slideReady twists (existence, via HasColoringFraction); (7) agreement/existence/uniqueness on standard forms and slideReady twists, plus all-rational agreement on the coloring-ready neighborhood (theorem4_all_rational_agreement: every non-monochrome coloring of a diagram with a ColoringIsotopy path from the diagram to a slideReady twist has fraction \(F\)) and existence there in the reversible direction (the colorFrom coloring transports forward along the symmetric path; exists_coloring_fraction_reversible_slideReady — one-way ColoringIsotopy from the twist cannot supply source colorings, so the reversible hypothesis is sharp — while one-way paths toward a diagram do supply them (exists_coloring_fraction_isotopy_from_slideReady). Diagonal sum on an arbitrary rational diagram (transport along unrestricted flype_slide_* or the switch-based generators, or addLeft/mulTop without port hypotheses) remains outstanding — and the port side is now known-sharp, not merely unproved. Part (2) is formalized generator-by-generator (affine freedom, Reidemeister I–III, flypes, colorability — see proof dependencies); the single-statement assembly "for every isotopy" is not claimed, since transport along unrestricted flype_slide_* and switch-based generators is outstanding. Part (7) past the coloring-ready neighborhood — arbitrary rational diagrams related only by a full-Isotopic witness, or non-slideReady parses — is likewise outstanding for the same reason.

Sketch, following the paper. Colorings of \([0]\) and \([1]\) give \(f([0])=0/1\), \(f([\infty])=1/0\), \(f([1])=1\), so (7) follows from (3), (5) and induction on twist form. For (1), the matrices of \([0]\) and \([\infty]\) have two equal rows or two equal columns; if \(T\) has matrix \(M\) satisfying the rule, then \(T+[1]\) has matrix \(\begin{pmatrix}a&2b-d\\c&b\end{pmatrix}\), and \(a+b=(2b-d)+c\) is equivalent to \(a+d=b+c\). The same holds for a negative twist and for a twist on the left, bottom, or top. For (2), \(f\) is unchanged by \(M\mapsto nM+k\) with \(n\neq 0\), and for a fixed coloring the external colors (hence \(f\)) survive Reidemeister moves and flypes. For (3), the right column of \(M(T)\) equals the left column of \(M(S)\), and the diagonal sum for \(S\) gives \(b-d=e-f\), whence \(f(T)+f(S)=(b-a)/(b-d)+(e-b)/(e-f)=(e-a)/(e-f)=f(T+S)\). For (4), \(M(-1/T)=M(T^r)=\begin{pmatrix}b&d\\a&c\end{pmatrix}\), so \(f(-1/T)=(d-b)/(d-c)=-1/f(T)\). For (5), the vertical reflect \(T':=(-T)^{v\mathrm{flip}}\) inherits a coloring with matrix \(\begin{pmatrix}b&a\\d&c\end{pmatrix}\), hence \(f(T')=-f(T)\), and \(T'\sim -T\) by the flipping lemma. Property (6) is (4) and (5).

The positive invert-add ladder closes at once: every non-monochrome coloring of (unitChain n).invert has fraction 1/(n+2). Rung n is the left-nested sum of n+2 positive units, so this covers the two-unit rung at 1/2 through all higher rungs, subsuming the per-rung values of the two/three/four/five-unit nodes. The step algebra is the per-rung pattern: the new numerator equals the old one while the new denominator gains one more multiple, with the nonzero transfers via mul_ne_zero. docs.title: Negative invert-add ladder
docs.text:
Per-rung values of the negative unit ladder: ([-1]×n)ⁱ carries -1/n. Each rung is proved directly — the switched rules force numerator d and denominator -nd — with the neg_ne_zero pattern for the negative denominator multiple, one pull-request-sized node each (the six-unit rung is split into universal and existence nodes for size; the ten-unit rung and above additionally factor their rule equations into a shared preliminaries node so each universal stays under the span limit, and live in the factored-rungs sub-chapter, continued in factored rungs two, factored rungs three, factored rungs four, factored rungs five, and factored rungs six).

Theorem32Unrestricted negative three-unit invert-add value#✓fully proved

Every non-monochrome coloring of ([-1]+[-1]+[-1])ⁱ has fraction -1/3 (universal), with a direct witness for the existence: the three switched rules force numerator d and denominator -3d for nonzero d, with no DiagonalSum or port inputs. The negative units are mirror-switches of the positive ones, so the arc wirings — and the sign of the denominator multiple — differ from the +1/3 case; the nonzero transfer additionally needs neg_ne_zero since the denominator multiple is negative. docs.title: Negative invert-add ladder: factored rungs six
docs.text:
Rungs thirty-five and above of the negative unit ladder, each split into crossings preliminaries, a fraction-value preliminary, universal, witness, witness-rules, existence, and (from rung thirty-six) witness-value nodes (the flat universal would otherwise exceed the span limit, and from rung twenty-nine the universal linarith tail is factored out the same way; from rung thirty-six the existence tail is factored likewise). Opened as the sequel of the factored-rungs-five sub-chapter, which holds 19 articles (a sextet cannot fit there: 19 + 6 = 25 > 24), so new rungs go here; the mathematics is unchanged.

Formalization progress3 definitions · 17 results20 fully proved

docs.title: Tangle foundations
docs.text:
Definitions for the combinatorial theory of rational 2-tangles: Reidemeister moves, 2-tangles and isotopy, integer and rational tangles, flypes and flips, standard, continued-fraction, and canonical forms, the arithmetic continued fraction, and the fraction \(F(T)\) as the arithmetical evaluation of the twist form.

Formalization progress11 definitions11 fully proved

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text:
Inductive1Reidemeister moves#✓fully proved

A Reidemeister move is one of the three local diagram changes R1, R2, R3 on a tangle (or knot) diagram, performed in the interior of the projection disc and leaving the four endpoints of a 2-tangle fixed.

  • R1. A kink may be added to or removed from a single strand (a twist of writhe \(\pm 1\)).
  • R2. Two strands with two opposite crossings may be pulled apart, or two uncrossed strands may be overlapped to create two opposite crossings.
  • R3. A strand may be slid over (or under) a crossing of two other strands.

Kauffman–Lambropoulou use these moves without listing the three pictures: isotopy of 2-tangle diagrams is equivalent to a finite sequence of Reidemeister moves in the interior of the disc (Introduction, arXiv PDF p. 2, citing Reidemeister [31]). Section 5 uses the same moves as the generators of diagram isotopy for coloring. This article spells out R1–R3 so that those uses are formalizable leaves rather than an imported axiom.

Planar isotopy of the diagram (no change of crossing data) is included with the Reidemeister generators.

Dependencies Used byLemma 3 (Coloring invariance under Reidemeister I) · Lemma 4 (Coloring invariance under Reidemeister II) · Lemma 5 (Coloring invariance under Reidemeister III) · Inductive 2 (2-tangle and isotopy) Inductive22-tangle and isotopy#✓fully proved

A 2-tangle is an embedding in a 3-ball \(B^3\) of two arcs and a finite number of circles, with the four endpoints of the arcs lying on \(\partial B^3\) in the standard NW/NE/SW/SE positions. (Throughout, “tangle” means a tangle diagram, as in the paper.)

Two rational tangles \(T,S\) in \(B^3\) are isotopic, written \(T\sim S\), if there is an orientation-preserving self-homeomorphism \(h:(B^3,T)\to(B^3,S)\) that is the identity on the boundary. Equivalently, any two diagrams of \(T\) and \(S\) have identical endpoint configurations on the projection disc and differ by a finite sequence of Reidemeister moves in the interior of the disc.

The class of 2-tangles is closed under addition \(T+S\), multiplication \(T\ast S\), mirror image \(-T\), rotation \(T^r\) (counterclockwise by \(90^\circ\)), and inversion \(T^i:=-T^r\). Numerator and denominator closures \(N(T)\) and \(D(T)\) produce knots or links; they are used later to form vertex closures, but are not themselves first-milestone targets.

The simplest rational tangles are \([0]\), \([\infty]\), \([+1]\) and \([-1]\). The next simplest are:

  • the integer tangles \([n]\), made of \(n\) horizontal twists, \(n\in\mathbb{Z}\);
  • the vertical tangles \([n]^{-1}\), made of \(n\) vertical twists, \(n\in\mathbb{Z}\).

Crossing type follows the checkerboard shading of the paper (Figure 2): positive type as in \([+1]\), negative type as in \([-1]\). These sign conventions agree with Ernst–Sumners and are the opposite of Conway 1970; this project follows Kauffman–Lambropoulou.

In particular \([0]^r=[0]^i=[\infty]\) and \([\infty]^r=[\infty]^i=[0]\), and \(-[n]=[-n]\).

The stacked diagram of \(|n|\) vertical twists below \([\infty]\) is the right-and-bottom picture of Conway \([n]^i=1/[n]\). It is not the PD-code of inverting \([n]\), which mirrors every crossing.

addLeft and mulTop) Definition5Rational tangle#✓fully proved

A rational tangle in twist form is created by consecutive additions and multiplications by the tangles \([\pm 1]\), starting from \([0]\) or \([\infty]\) (Definition 1). Equivalently (Note 1), it is a proper embedding of two unoriented arcs \(\alpha_1,\alpha_2\) in a 3-ball \(B^3\) with four endpoints on the boundary for which there exists a homeomorphism of pairs $$ h:(B^3,\alpha_1,\alpha_2)\longrightarrow(D^2\times I,{x,y}\times I) $$ to a trivial tangle.

Inductively, a twist-form rational tangle is obtained from a previously created rational tangle by adding integer tangles and multiplying by vertical tangles. Addition or multiplication of two non-integer rational tangles need not remain rational.

This project takes Definition 1 as the working definition of a rational tangle, with the homeomorphism-of-pairs description as the intended topological meaning.

A flype is an isotopy of a 2-tangle or a knot applied on a 2-subtangle of the form \([\pm 1]+t\) or \([\pm 1]\ast t\) as in Figure 5 of the paper. It fixes the endpoints of the subtangle on which it is applied. A flype is rational if that 2-subtangle is rational.

Algebraically (after the flipping lemma), a rational flype is one of $$ [\pm 1]+t \;\sim\; t+[\pm 1] \qquad\text{or}\qquad [\pm 1]\ast t \;\sim\; t\ast[\pm 1]. $$

A tangle (or knot) diagram is alternating when the crossings alternate from under to over along every arc; equivalently, with the paper's checkerboard shading, when all crossings have the same type. Flypes preserve the alternating structure. Lemma 1 and Corollary 1 of the paper record that every 2-subtangle of a rational tangle in twist form is a rational truncation, so every flype of a rational tangle is rational.

A flip is a rotation in space of a 2-tangle by \(180^\circ\).

  • \(T^{h\mathrm{flip}}\) is the horizontal flip: rotation around a horizontal axis in the plane of \(T\).
  • \(T^{v\mathrm{flip}}\) is the vertical flip: rotation around a vertical axis in the plane of \(T\).

In general a flip switches endpoints and need not be an isotopy of 2-tangles. For rational tangles it is, by the flipping lemma. A flype on a 2-subtangle \(t\) may be written $$ [\pm 1]+t \;\sim\; t^{h\mathrm{flip}}+[\pm 1] \qquad\text{or}\qquad [\pm 1]\ast t \;\sim\; t^{v\mathrm{flip}}\ast[\pm 1]. $$

A rational tangle is in standard form if it is created by consecutive additions of \([\pm 1]\) only on the right (or only on the left) and multiplications by \([\pm 1]\) only at the bottom (or only at the top), starting from \([0]\) or \([\infty]\) (Definition 4).

Inductively, from a previously created rational tangle \(T\), one either adds an integer tangle on the right, \(T\mapsto T+[\pm k]\), or multiplies by a vertical tangle at the bottom, \(T\mapsto T\ast[n]^{-1}\). The associated integer vector \((a_1,\ldots,a_n)\) records the successive blocks of twists; \(n\) may be taken odd.

A continued fraction in integer tangles is an algebraic description of a rational tangle via a continued fraction built from integer tangles \([a_1],\ldots,[a_n]\) with all numerators equal to \(1\): $$ T = [[a_1],[a_2],\ldots,[a_n]] := [a_1] + \cfrac{1}{[a_2]+\cdots+\cfrac{1}{[a_n]}} $$ for \(a_2,\ldots,a_n\in\mathbb{Z}\setminus\{0\}\) and \(n\) even or odd. The leading term \(a_1\) may be zero. A rational tangle so described is in continued fraction form.

This is the tangle-level counterpart of the arithmetic continued fraction \([a_1,\ldots,a_n]\). Lemma 5 of the paper records the effect of adding \([\pm 1]\), inverting, and mirroring on the continued-fraction vector.

A rational tangle \(T=[[\beta_1],[\beta_2],\ldots,[\beta_m]]\) in continued fraction form is in canonical form if \(T\) is alternating (all \(\beta_i\) positive, or all negative) and \(m\) is odd (Definition 6). If \(T\) is alternating and \(m\) is even, the last term may be split by the identity \([\beta_m]=[\mathrm{sign}(\beta_m)\cdot(|\beta_m|-1)]+[\mathrm{sign}(\beta_m)\cdot 1]\) to make the length odd.

\(T\) is called positive or negative according to the sign of its terms.

Every rational number may be written as a continued fraction with all numerators equal to \(1\): $$ [a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_n] := a_1 + \cfrac{1}{a_2+\cdots+\cfrac{1}{a_n}} $$ for \(a_1\in\mathbb{Z}\) and \(a_2,\ldots,a_n\in\mathbb{Z}\setminus\{0\}\). The leading term \(a_1\) may be zero. The length is \(n\) whether or not \(a_1=0\).

A continued fraction is termwise positive (resp. negative) if every numerical term is positive (resp. negative). It is in canonical form (Definition 7) if it is termwise positive or negative and the length \(m\) is odd. Even length is reduced to odd length by the last-term identities \([a_1,\ldots,a_n]=[a_1,\ldots,a_n-1,+1]\) for \(a_n>0\) and \([a_1,\ldots,a_n]=[a_1,\ldots,a_n+1,-1]\) for \(a_n<0\).

The value \(\infty\) is included formally as \(1/0\), matching \(F([\infty])\).

Mathlib already develops generalised, simple, and regular continued fractions under Algebra.ContinuedFractions (including GenContFract.of and termination iff rationality). That overlap is arithmetic, not a tangle theory; it is recorded as a candidate, not as mathlib: true.

Dependencies Used byDefinition 8 (Fraction of a rational tangle) · Theorem 172 (Unique canonical continued fraction) Definition8Fraction of a rational tangle#✓fully proved

Let \(T\) be a rational tangle in twist form. The fraction \(F(T)\) is the rational number (or \(\infty\)) obtained by evaluating that expression in ordinary arithmetic, with the tangle product interpreted as $$ x\ast y := \frac{1}{\frac{1}{x}+y}, $$ and with \(F([\infty]):=\infty=1/0\) as a formal expression (Definition 8).

By Remark 6, if \(T=[[a_1],\ldots,[a_n]]\) is in continued fraction form then $$ F(T)=[a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_n], $$ and this evaluation may be taken as the definition of \(F(T)\). In particular \(F([0])=0\), \(F([\pm 1])=\pm 1\), \(F([\pm k])=\pm k\), and \(F([{\pm k}]^{-1})=1/(\pm k)\).

Lemma 7 of the paper shows that the twist-form and continued-fraction-form evaluations agree. Lemma 8 records the calculus \(F(T+[\pm 1])=F(T)\pm 1\), \(F(T^{-1})=1/F(T)\), \(F(-T)=-F(T)\).

Theorem180Uniqueness of the coloring fraction on larger honest classes#✓fully proved

On a slideReady twist diagram every non-monochrome integral coloring has coloring fraction equal to the standard-form value, so any two agree. On a right-and-bottom twist the same uniqueness holds with value equal to the arithmetical fraction of the expression (the diagonal-sum rule is discharged).

On addLeft (resp. mulTop) of a right-and-bottom inner expression, with the same non-degenerate glue used to color those constructors (\(NW eq SW\) / \(NW eq NE\)), every non-monochrome coloring has fraction equal to the arithmetical value (resp. the standard-form value: top Conway product need not equal algebraic mulTop.fraction). Affine uniqueness of colorFrom extends to those constructors, so the colorFrom family shares that value. Uniqueness of arbitrary colorings without the port hypotheses is not claimed: DiagonalSum/slideReady need distinct glue ports.

If a diagram is related by ColoringIsotopy to a slideReady twist (the twist is the target), transport preserves the color matrix, hence the coloring fraction equals that standard-form value. The reverse one-way direction is not claimed: unrestricted dummy-strand zero_add and one-way glue do not reverse. On the reversible fragment the path may be reversed, so uniqueness holds in both directions.

On a two-block PD-sum of integer diagrams, restriction of a non-monochrome coloring to each summand is non-monochrome (a monochrome summand would force the other summand or the sum to be monochrome, or would force an infinite integer fraction). Additivity of the coloring fraction then gives the value \(n+m\).

This is not uniqueness on an arbitrary diagram. A TwistExpr that is not slideReady (including addLeft/mulTop without port hypotheses) is omitted. Unrestricted flype-slides (no diagonal-sum or port hypotheses) are omitted, and are not added to ColoringIsotopy. This article does not claim isotopy invariance of the arithmetical fraction.

The §4 flyping proof of Theorem 2, which uses the Tait conjecture as background, is retained as exposition and is marked out of the coverage contract for this milestone. Nothing on the path to Theorem 1 depends on these articles.

Theorem159Tait flyping conjecture#●ready to state

Two alternating knots are isotopic if and only if any two corresponding diagrams on \(S^2\) are related by a finite sequence of flypes.

This is Tait's 1877 working assumption, proved by Menasco and Thistlethwaite in 1993. Kauffman–Lambropoulou assume the corresponding statement for vertex closures of alternating 2-tangles (citing Thistlethwaite) and derive from it the flyping statement for alternating rational tangles (Proposition 4). The result is background, not a theorem proved in the adopted paper.

This article is retained as exposition of the unused §4 flyping argument. It is not a dependency of Theorem 1: the classification is proved via the coloring fraction of §5. Tait is not an axiom on the critical path.

Dependencies Statement usesInductive 3 (Flype) · Inductive 2 (2-tangle and isotopy) Used byTheorem 160 (Alternating rational tangles related by flypes) Theorem160Alternating rational tangles related by flypes#●ready to state

Two alternating rational tangles on \(S^2\) are isotopic if and only if they differ by a finite sequence of rational flypes.

The argument passes to the vertex closure \(V(T)\) of an alternating rational tangle, invokes the Tait flyping theorem for that closure, and reconfigures any flype that involves the rigid vertex as a pancake flip plus a tangle flype. Pancake flips induce horizontal or vertical flips, which the paper treats as isotopies of rational tangles; note the formalized flipping lemma covers only the coloring-honest fragment (planar rotation, not \(h\mathrm{flip}\)/v\mathrm{flip} as diagram isotopies), so this step has no Lean backing. Remaining tangle flypes are rational by Corollary 1.

This article is retained as exposition of the unused §4 flyping argument. It is not a dependency of Theorem 1.

Theorem171The fraction is an isotopy invariant#✓fully proved

The fraction \(F\) is an isotopy invariant of rational tangles: if \(T\sim S\) are rational, then \(F(T)=F(S)\).

This is Theorem 2. The proof used in this DAG is the coloring argument of §5, not the flyping argument of §4. By Theorem 4, \(f\) is a topological invariant of rational tangles and \(f(T)=F(T)\). Therefore \(F\) is an isotopy invariant.

There is no appeal to the Tait flyping conjecture or to Proposition 4.

Dependencies Statement usesDefinition 8 (Fraction of a rational tangle) · Inductive 2 (2-tangle and isotopy) Proof usesTheorem 3 (Coloring fraction of a rational tangle) Used byTheorem 177 (Classification of rational tangles) · Theorem 178 (Same fraction implies isotopic) Theorem178Same fraction implies isotopic#●ready to prove

Two rational tangles with the same fraction are isotopic.

Let \(T=[[a_1],\ldots,[a_n]]\) and \(S=[[b_1],\ldots,[b_m]]\) satisfy \(F(T)=F(S)=p/q\). Bring each to canonical form \(T'\) and \(S'\). Invariance of \(F\) gives \(F(T')=F(S')=p/q\). Proposition 3 supplies a unique arithmetic canonical expansion \(p/q=[\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_r]\), hence a unique alternating rational tangle \(Q=[[\gamma_1],\ldots,[\gamma_r]]\) in canonical form. If \(T'\neq Q\) then two distinct canonical continued fractions would evaluate to \(p/q\), contradicting Proposition 3. Thus \(T'=Q=S'\), so \(T\sim S\).

Two rational tangles are isotopic if and only if they have the same fraction.

This is Theorem 1 of Kauffman–Lambropoulou, attributed to Conway (1970). The paper states it in the Introduction. This DAG obtains it as the conjunction of Theorem 2 (the fraction is an isotopy invariant, via the coloring fraction \(f\) of Theorem 4) and Theorem 3 (equal fractions yield isotopic tangles, from §4). Tait flyping and Proposition 4 are not used.

docs.text:
Formalized for twist-form expressions whose fraction agrees with the standard-form evaluation: unconditionally on noMulTop (hence on rightBottom) expressions, and conditionally in general (twist_same_fraction_isotopic records the exact hypotheses). Diagram-level uniqueness of the standard-form value holds for right-and-bottom parses of one PD-code. Diagram-level elimination of top products is now proved: toNoMulTop isotopes any twist diagram to a noMulTop one (toNoMulTop_isotopic via flype_mul + isotopic_rot180) preserving the standard-form fraction (toNoMulTop_toStandard_fraction). What remains outstanding for the unrestricted mulTop case is algebraic TwistExpr.fraction preservation in general — the commutativity hypothesis is now discharged when the inner fraction is ±1 (mulTop_comm_of_unit_fraction, claimed with the twist-diagram fraction results) — and coloring transport along the normalization path, so this node is not yet marked proved. The boundary is now sharp, not merely outstanding: the agreement hypotheses are necessary in general, since a mulTop node over inner fraction 2 has algebraic F = 1/3 against standard-form 2/3 (see the fixed-point sharpness).

On right-and-bottom parses the fraction is a function of the PD-code (exists_unique_fraction_rightBottom, relationally, so no choice principle), and same fraction implies isotopic at diagram level for rightBottom-parseable diagrams (same_fraction_isotopic_rightBottom). The same holds on noMulTop slideReady parses (exists_unique_fraction_noMulTop, same_fraction_isotopic_noMulTop; the colorFrom discharge needs slideReady, while isotopy needs only noMulTop). Arbitrary parses and arbitrary rational diagrams remain outstanding.

Formalized on the proved fragment (rational_classification_fragment): along ColoringIsotopy between noMulTop slideReady twists, algebraic fractions agree (forward invariance, via colorFrom) and equal fractions give isotopic diagrams (reconstruction). The forward direction rests on the coloring-ready invariance assembly, via the noMulTop colorFrom discharge (fraction_ColoringIsotopy_noMulTop_colorFrom); the converse on the noMulTop twist same-fraction reconstruction (twist_same_fraction_isotopic_of_noMulTop). The general same-fraction node is parked and is not used.

Beyond the fragment: full Isotopic invariance in either direction is not claimed. Unrestricted flype_slide_* and the switch-based generators are unproved, and several transports are refuted outright — matrix-preserving mirror transport (mirror refutation), invert transport on two crossings (invert refutation), and the diagonal rule without port hypotheses (diagonal sharpness). So this node is marked proved on the ColoringIsotopy/noMulTop/slideReady fragment only.

Note 2 then records the bijection: if \(T=[[a_1],\ldots,[a_n]]\) and \(p/q=[a_1,\ldots,a_n]\), one may write \(T=[p/q]\) without ambiguity. Rational numbers (together with \(\infty\)) are thus represented bijectively by rational tangles; negatives correspond to mirrors and inverses to inverses. That bijection is a corollary of this theorem, not a separate first-milestone target.

docs.title: Normal forms
docs.text:
Standard form, continued-fraction form, and canonical form are reached by flypes (as isotopies proved in the paper, not via Tait). The arithmetic continued fraction of a rational has a unique canonical form (Proposition 3), which is the numerical counterpart of the tangle canonical form and is used in Theorem 3.

Formalization progress9 results9 fully proved

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
Lemma12Every rational tangle has a standard form#✓fully proved

Every rational tangle can be brought via isotopy to standard form.

Starting from twist form, horizontal and vertical rational flypes (and the commutativity supplied by the flipping lemma) move all horizontal twists to the right and all vertical twists to the bottom.

Dependencies Statement usesDefinition 6 (Standard form) Proof usesInductive 3 (Flype) · Lemma 8 (Flipping lemma) Used byTheorem 173 (Every rational tangle has a continued fraction form) · Theorem 167 (Standard-form value of a twist diagram is well-defined) · Theorem 176 (Twist expressions of equal fraction are isotopic) Theorem173Every rational tangle has a continued fraction form#✓fully proved

Every rational tangle can be written in continued fraction form.

The argument reduces to standard form (Lemma 3) and then applies the isotopy identities of Lemma 4, $$ T\ast[n]^{-1} \;\sim\; \bigl([n]+T^{-1}\bigr)^{-1}, $$ repeatedly, converting a standard-form tangle into \([[a_1],\ldots,[a_n]]\). Thus continued-fraction form and standard form are equivalent presentations.

Dependencies Statement usesDefinition 7 (Continued fraction form) Proof usesLemma 12 (Every rational tangle has a standard form) Used byTheorem 174 (Every rational tangle isotopes to canonical form) · Theorem 175 (Canonical diagrams of equal fraction are equal) Theorem174Every rational tangle isotopes to canonical form#✓fully proved

Every rational tangle can be isotoped to canonical form: an alternating continued-fraction form of odd length.

If a continued-fraction vector is not termwise of one sign, a transfer move (Figure 14) together with flypes and flips removes a mixed-sign adjacent pair and reduces the sum of absolute values of the entries, so induction produces an alternating tangle. Length is then made odd by splitting the last term as in Definition 6.

Dependencies Statement usesDefinition 25 (Canonical form of a rational tangle) Proof usesTheorem 173 (Every rational tangle has a continued fraction form) · Inductive 3 (Flype) · Lemma 8 (Flipping lemma) Used byTheorem 178 (Same fraction implies isotopic) · Theorem 175 (Canonical diagrams of equal fraction are equal) Theorem172Unique canonical continued fraction#✓fully proved

Every continued fraction \([a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_n]\) can be transformed to a unique canonical form, with sign generically equal to the sign of the first non-zero term.

The reduction copies the transfer arithmetic of Proposition 2: mixed-sign adjacent terms are rewritten so that the sum of absolute values of the entries drops by one. The remaining uniqueness is Euclid's algorithm (Kauffman–Lambropoulou, end of the proof of Proposition 3). Even length is reduced to odd length by the last-term identities of Remark 5.

This is the arithmetic counterpart of the tangle canonical form, and is the unicity of continued-fraction form used in Theorem 3.

Dependencies Statement usesStructure 2 (Arithmetic continued fraction) Used byTheorem 178 (Same fraction implies isotopic) · Theorem 175 (Canonical diagrams of equal fraction are equal) Theorem175Canonical diagrams of equal fraction are equal#✓fully proved

Two tangles already in canonical continued-fraction form with the same arithmetic value are the same diagram: uniqueness of the odd-length one-sign expansion (Proposition 3) supplies a unique canonicalCF q, so both diagrams are (canonicalCF q).tangle and hence isotopic. The remaining canonical form of value \(\infty\) is \([\infty]\).

A standard-form expression with finite fraction \(q\) isotopes to that unique diagram. The reduction is the transfer / last-term rewrite of Proposition 2, shown to preserve the arithmetic value, so the resulting canonical expansion is canonicalCF q rather than an unspecified alternating tangle. Two standard forms of the same finite fraction are therefore isotopic (and likewise for value \(\infty\)).

This is strictly smaller than Theorem 3: it does not apply to an arbitrary rational tangle, and it does not claim that \(F\) is invariant under leftover Isotopic generators.

Dependencies Statement usesDefinition 25 (Canonical form of a rational tangle) · Definition 8 (Fraction of a rational tangle) · Definition 6 (Standard form) · Theorem 172 (Unique canonical continued fraction) Proof usesTheorem 174 (Every rational tangle isotopes to canonical form) · Theorem 173 (Every rational tangle has a continued fraction form) Used byTheorem 176 (Twist expressions of equal fraction are isotopic) Theorem176Twist expressions of equal fraction are isotopic#✓fully proved

Two twist-form expressions with the same arithmetical fraction \(F\) have isotopic diagrams, provided each expression's \(F\) agrees with the right-and-bottom evaluation of toStandard.

The diagrams first isotope to standard form by the slides already in toStandard_isotopic (horizontal and vertical rational flypes, including left addition and top multiplication). Standard forms of a given finite value (or of \(\infty\)) then isotope to one another by uniqueness of the canonical continued fraction. Algebraic \(F\) equals that standard-form value on every expression that never uses a top product: addition is commutative, so left addition is allowed, while the Conway product is not commutative.

This is strictly smaller than Theorem 3. It does not apply to an arbitrary rational diagram (an Isotopic witness of IsRational), and it does not claim that \(F\) is well-defined along leftover Isotopic generators.

Dependencies Statement usesDefinition 8 (Fraction of a rational tangle) · Definition 6 (Standard form) · Definition 25 (Canonical form of a rational tangle) Proof usesTheorem 175 (Canonical diagrams of equal fraction are equal) · Lemma 12 (Every rational tangle has a standard form) Used byTheorem 177 (Classification of rational tangles) Theorem167Standard-form value of a twist diagram is well-defined#✓fully proved

If two twist-form expressions denote the same PD-code, they have the same standard-form evaluation toStandard.fraction, once each expression is slideReady and a non-monochrome coloring of that code satisfies the diagonal-sum rule. The coloring fraction of the diagram equals each expression's standard-form value, so that value is a function of the diagram rather than of the expression tree.

On right-and-bottom expressions the coloring is constructed by propagating two initial strand colors, so no extra coloring hypothesis remains, and algebraic \(F\) agrees with the standard-form value. On noMulTop slideReady expressions the coloring hypotheses likewise discharge by colorFrom, for both the standard-form and the algebraic value. The mulTop commutativity hypothesis itself holds when the inner fraction is ±1 (the fixed points of inv: both sides reduce to s ± 1), so mulTop over a unit-fraction twist preserves algebraic F — and on the unitMulTop subclass (every top product over a ±1 inner) the toNoMulTop normalization preserves algebraic F throughout, giving a noMulTop expression with identical F for Theorem 3.

A diagram that is a twist-form PD-code may therefore be assigned this standard-form value via any right-and-bottom parse. An IsRational witness is an isotopy to a twist diagram, not PD-code equality; assigning \(F\) to an arbitrary rational diagram still requires isotopy invariance (Theorem 2).

This is not Theorem 2, Theorem 3, or Theorem 4.

Dependencies Statement usesDefinition 8 (Fraction of a rational tangle) · Definition 6 (Standard form) · Definition 5 (Rational tangle) Proof usesTheorem 3 (Coloring fraction of a rational tangle) · Lemma 12 (Every rational tangle has a standard form) Used byTheorem 168 (Standard-form $F$ along coloring isotopy) Theorem168Standard-form $F$ along coloring isotopy#✓fully proved

If two slideReady twist-form expressions are related by ColoringIsotopy and the source admits a non-monochrome coloring that satisfies the diagonal sum rule, then they have the same standard-form evaluation toStandard.fraction. The coloring fraction of each diagram equals that value, and coloring fraction is already invariant along ColoringIsotopy.

On expressions with no top product the same conclusion holds for algebraic \(F\). On right-and-bottom expressions the coloring is colorFrom, so no extra coloring hypothesis remains; the colorFrom discharge now also covers all noMulTop slideReady expressions (fraction_ColoringIsotopy_noMulTop_colorFrom).

This is not Theorem 2: ColoringIsotopy does not include unrestricted Figure 14 transfers, flype-slides, or invert_cong, and it is not full diagram isotopy. Assigning \(F\) to an arbitrary rational diagram still requires isotopy invariance of \(F\).

The mulTop commutativity equation \((s^{-1}+F)^{-1}=(F^{-1}+s)^{-1}\) holds exactly at \(F=\pm 1\) (per sign, hence jointly): \(0\) and \(\infty\) fail by direct computation, and for finite nonzero values injectivity of inv reduces the equation to \(q=q^{-1}\), i.e. \(q^2=1\). Together with the sufficiency direction, the unit-fraction hypothesis for mulTop normalization is therefore both necessary and sufficient on finite values — blocker (b) is closed on the finiteness fragment. The necessity is sharp at expression level: on mulTop (addRight one pos) pos (inner fraction \(2\)), algebraic \(F\) is \(1/3\) while the standard-form evaluation is \(2/3\) (mulTop_two_inner_ne_toStandard), so the agreement hypotheses of twist_same_fraction_isotopic cannot be dropped in general.

Theorem216Canceling two-block sums and products#✓fully proved

The two-block PD-sum (integerTangle n).add (integerTangle (-n)) is not a TwistExpr; gluing integer colorings gives fraction \(0\) when non-monochrome, and invert-add reuses coloring_invert_add_two_rightBottom for \(n eq 0\) (summands of finite nonzero \(F\)) or the [0] lemmas for \(n = 0\), carrying \(\infty\). Dually, the two-block PD-product (verticalTwists n).mul (verticalTwists (-n)) carries \(\infty\), and invert-mul carries \(0\). The general two-block glue (coloring_mul_two_rightBottom) and mirror (coloring_mirror_mul_two) machines are claimed here.

This is not a ColoringIsotopy constructor: invert-add/invert-mul switch crossings. It is not unrestricted flype_slide, not invert_cong on ColoringIsotopy, and not Theorem 2.
